opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and honestly I think it's one where the answer is still evolving. In my own work, mostly on legged locomotion, the reward has traditionally been fairly self-contained: track a velocity command, don't fall, keep the joint torques and accelerations reasonable, avoid collisions with the terrain. Once you put a robot around people, though, the reward stops being only about the robot and starts being about the people too.

I'd separate it into a few layers. The first is the hard stuff, safety. Things like minimum distance to humans, limits on speed and contact forces near people, and avoiding fast motions in shared spaces. I'm actually a bit skeptical of encoding those purely as reward terms, because a policy will happily trade a small penalty for a big gain elsewhere if the weighting allows it. So I'd rather treat them as constraints, either through constrained RL formulations, through termination conditions during training, or through a separate safety layer that can override the learned policy. The reward shapes behavior, but it shouldn't be the only thing standing between the robot and someone's shin.

The second layer is the task itself: get to the goal, carry the object, follow the person. That part is relatively easy to define, and it's usually the part people over-optimize.

The third layer is the hardest and the most interesting: being legible and comfortable to be around. A robot can be perfectly safe in a collision sense and still be really unpleasant, because it cuts close in front of you, hesitates unpredictably, or moves in ways you can't anticipate. Hand-crafting a reward for that is tricky. You can add proxies like smoothness, predictable heading, and respecting personal space, and passing on the expected side in a corridor, but I think this is where learning from human data helps a lot, either through preference feedback or by modeling how people actually move and react. Ideally you want humans in the loop telling you which behaviors feel right, rather than an engineer guessing at weights.

The practical catch is that RL needs a lot of interaction data, and you can't run millions of episodes with real people. So you're simulating humans, and your reward is only as good as your human model. A policy trained against simulated pedestrians that behave too politely or too predictably can learn to exploit them, for example assuming people will always get out of the way. So part of the reward design question is really a simulation design question: making the human agents diverse and sometimes uncooperative enough that the robot learns to be robust instead of pushy.

So, in short: put safety in constraints rather than leaving it to a weighted reward term, keep the task reward simple, and learn the social-comfort part from human feedback as much as possible. Then put a lot of effort into the realism of the humans in your simulation, because that's where the reward actually gets its meaning.

r001.rationale: The response recommends limiting speed and avoiding fast motions near people, but does not say that fast movement makes humans perceive robots as dangerous.

r002.rationale: It notes that a policy may trade a safety penalty for a larger gain and that task objectives can be over-optimized, but does not explain that reward optimization may make the robot reach its goal faster than is desirable around humans.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the harder parts of the whole problem. In our locomotion work, reward design is already tricky, but there you're mostly dealing with the robot's own body: you want it to track a velocity command, keep its base stable, not slam its feet into the ground, keep the motion smooth and energy-efficient. Those are things you can measure directly from the simulator state, and you can iterate quickly because you have thousands of environments running in parallel.

Once you put humans in the loop, the reward has to capture things that are much less well-defined. The first thing I'd say is that safety shouldn't really be a reward term in the usual sense, where it just gets traded off against everything else. If you put a negative reward on collisions and a positive reward on reaching the goal, the policy will happily learn that a small probability of bumping into someone is worth it if it gets to the goal faster. So I think you want hard constraints, or at least very heavily weighted terms, for things like minimum distance to people and not approaching them head-on at high speed. And ideally you back that up with something outside the policy, a safety layer that can override it.

The second part is that the behavior around humans needs to be predictable, not just collision-free. A robot that technically never hits anyone but constantly changes direction, or stops abruptly right in front of you, is unpleasant and people don't trust it. So I'd include terms that penalize jerky velocity changes, reward keeping a consistent path, and encourage passing on a consistent side. A lot of that comes from the social navigation literature, where people have studied what humans actually find comfortable.

The third thing, and this is where simulation gets hard, is that you need a reasonable model of how humans move in the first place. If your human agents in sim just walk in straight lines, the policy will overfit to that. We've seen this in sim-to-real for locomotion: whatever you don't randomize or model, the policy exploits. So you want diverse, somewhat reactive human behavior in the training environment, and then your reward can include terms about not forcing humans to deviate from their path, which is a nice proxy for being a good citizen in a crowd.

And finally, I'd say the reward should be shaped so that the task component is simple. Reach the goal, don't take forever, don't burn energy. Keep the complexity in the safety and social terms, and keep it modular so you can inspect what each term is doing. In practice we spend a lot of time just watching rollouts and asking, why did it do that, and then tracing it back to one specific term. If the reward is a big tangle, you lose that ability, and around humans that's not acceptable.

r001.rationale: The response mentions avoiding high-speed, head-on approaches, but it does not say that fast robot movement makes humans perceive robots as dangerous.

r002.rationale: It explains that a policy may accept some collision risk if doing so lets it reach the goal faster, showing how reward optimization can favor excessive speed around people.

astra-6.text:
I think the important thing is that the reward shouldn’t just describe getting to the goal. If you reward the robot only for reaching a destination quickly, you might get behavior that is efficient but very uncomfortable for the people around it.

So you need to account for how it gets there: maintaining distance from people, moving smoothly, and behaving in a way that people can anticipate. And those objectives can conflict. A robot that stays completely still might be very safe in one sense, but it’s not particularly useful.

I would also separate preferences from safety requirements. You can use the reward to encourage considerate behavior, but a penalty for collisions doesn’t guarantee that collisions won’t happen. You need additional constraints or safeguards for that.

Then the difficult part is validating whether the reward actually captures what you intended. You have to look at the resulting behavior, including situations where people move unexpectedly, rather than just checking whether the policy achieves a high reward.

r001.rationale: The response says goal-seeking quickly can make behavior uncomfortable, but does not identify fast movement as a reason people perceive robots as dangerous.

r002.rationale: It explains that rewarding only reaching the destination quickly can produce behavior that is efficient but uncomfortable for people nearby.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is that the reward captures more than just reaching a goal as quickly as possible. If you only reward progress, the robot may discover behavior that is efficient but uncomfortable for the people around it. So you need to account for safety, keeping an appropriate distance, and moving in a way that people can understand and anticipate.

And some of those requirements probably shouldn’t just be reward terms. You don’t want the robot to trade off a collision against getting somewhere a little faster. You need constraints as well. Then, within those constraints, the reward can encourage useful, smooth, efficient behavior. The difficult part is making sure that what you specify actually corresponds to the behavior you want when the robot interacts with people.

r001.rationale: The response mentions safety, distance, and predictable movement, but does not say that fast movement makes people perceive robots as dangerous.

r002.rationale: It says a progress-only reward may favor reaching a goal as quickly as possible and produce efficient but uncomfortable behavior around people, conveying that optimizing for speed can be undesirable.
